title: The Caravan's Long Journey
summary: A merchant's son joins his father's trading caravan for the first time, learning how travelers navigated by the stars, managed their water with great care, and depended on trust between fellow merchants to cross the desert safely.
poll: Trusting other people is more important than being strong or clever when facing a hard journey.

versions.title: The Caravan's Long Journey
versions.text:
Faisal is a boy. His dad trades goods. His dad has a caravan.

A caravan is many camels. They walk in a line. They carry goods to sell.

Faisal goes on the trip. It is his first time. The camels cross the desert.

The desert is hot and dry. The men need water. They put water in bags.

At night, Faisal looks up. He sees stars. His dad shows him one star. "We walk toward that star," he says.

One day, wind comes fast. Sand flies all around! The men stop and wait.

After the wind, a man's bag has a leak. His water is almost gone. Other men give him some of theirs.

"We help each other," says Dad. "That is how we stay safe." At the end, they reach the market. Faisal sold goods. He is proud.

versions.title: The Caravan's Long Journey
versions.text:
Faisal is a boy. His father leads a trade caravan. A caravan is many camels. They walk together.

The camels carry goods to sell in far towns. This year, Faisal joins the trip. It is his first time. The caravan must cross a wide, dry desert.

The desert is very hot in the day. Water matters most of all. Each camel carries bags of water.

At night, Faisal looks up at the sky. He sees many bright stars. His father points to one star. "We walk toward that star," he says.

One day, a strong wind blows. Sand flies everywhere. The men cannot see far. They stop the camels and wait.

After the wind stops, one man finds a leak in his water bag. His water is almost gone. The other men share some water with him.

"We help each other," says Dad. "That is how a caravan stays safe." At last, they reach the market town. Faisal helps sell the goods.

After the wind stops, one man finds a leak in his water bag. His water is almost gone, and he looks worried. The other men quickly share some of their own water with him.

versions.title: The Caravan's Long Journey
versions.text:
Faisal is a boy. His father leads a trade caravan. It carries goods across the land, from town to town, during an old time long ago.

A caravan is a long line of camels that walk together, carrying bundles of goods to sell in far towns. This year, Faisal joins the trip for the first time, and the caravan must cross a wide, dry desert on an old trade road.

The desert grows very hot in the day. Water is the thing that matters most. Each camel carries bags of water on its back. The men must use the water with care, since no one knows when they will find more.

At night, Faisal looks up at the sky and sees many bright stars. His father points to one star. "We walk toward that star," he says. "It shows us the way when the land has no roads."

One day, a strong wind blows, and sand flies everywhere. The men stop the camels and wait. They cannot see far through the thick, blowing sand.

After the wind stops, one man finds a leak in his water bag. His water is almost gone. The other men quickly share some water with him, without being asked.

"We help each other on this road," says Faisal's father. "That is how a caravan stays safe." At last, they reach the market town. Faisal proudly helps sell the goods.

versions.title: The Caravan's Long Journey
versions.text:
Faisal had heard stories about his father's trade trips for years. This was the first time he was allowed to join the caravan himself, crossing the desert on an old route used by merchants for a very long time.

A caravan was a long line of camels that walked together, carrying bundles of goods such as spices between towns. The route had been used by merchants for hundreds of years. It wound past rocky hills and old wells that travelers depended on.

Each camel carried bags of water, since water mattered more than almost anything else in the desert. The men used it with great care. They never knew exactly when they would reach the next well or oasis.

At night, Faisal's father taught him to find his way by the stars. "That bright star shows the way," he said, "and so do landmarks, like that strange rock shaped like a camel's head."

One afternoon, a strong wind rose, and sand filled the air. The caravan stopped, and the men waited together. They could not see the landmarks they usually used to find their way.

After the wind died down, one merchant found that his water bag had torn open. He had almost no water left. The other traders shared their own water with him.

"Trust between merchants keeps a caravan alive," Faisal's father said. "No one crosses this desert alone." At last, the caravan reached the market town, and Faisal proudly helped sell the goods.

versions.title: The Caravan's Long Journey
versions.text:
Faisal had heard stories about his father's trading journeys for many years, but this was the first time he had been permitted to join the caravan himself, crossing the Arabian desert along an ancient incense route that merchants had followed for centuries.

A caravan consisted of a long line of camels walking together, carrying bundles of goods such as frankincense and cloth between distant towns. The route had been used by traders for centuries, winding past rocky hills and scattered wells that travelers depended upon to survive the difficult journey.

Each camel carried bags of water, since water was essential in a land where it remained scarce for long stretches at a time. The men used every drop with great care, never certain exactly when they would reach the next well or oasis.

At night, Faisal's father carefully taught him to navigate by watching the stars. "That bright star shows the way," he explained, "and so do landmarks, like that strange rock shaped like a camel's head."

One afternoon, a strong wind suddenly rose, and thick sand filled the air, hiding the horizon completely. The caravan stopped, and the men waited together, since they could no longer see the landmarks they depended upon to navigate.

After the wind died down, one merchant discovered that his water bag had torn open, leaving him with almost nothing. Without hesitation, the other traders cooperated at once, sharing their own scarce water with him.

"Merchants must cooperate and trust one another, or no caravan survives this desert," Faisal's father explained. At last, the caravan reached the market town, and Faisal proudly helped sell the frankincense they had carried the whole way.

That night, resting beside the fire, Faisal realized how much he had learned on this single journey. He now understood how to navigate by the stars and the landmarks, how to use scarce water with care, and how deeply every merchant in a caravan must trust the others around him.

LOW.modelAnswer: It is important for people in a caravan to help each other because the desert is a hard and dangerous place. When one man's water bag leaked, the other men shared their own water with him so he would not run out. Faisal's father says that this kind of help is how a caravan stays safe, since no one could cross the desert alone.

questions.stem: Why do the men use water with such great care?
options: They cannot be sure when they will find more
They do not like the taste of desert water
They plan to sell the water at market
The water belongs only to Faisal's father
questions.why: Since they never know exactly when they will reach the next well, they must ration their water carefully.

wrong.B: Taste is never mentioned in the story.
wrong.C: The caravan sells goods like spices, not water.
wrong.D: The water is shared among all the men, not owned by one person.

questions.stem: What can you infer about the merchants from how they treat the man with the leak?
options: They are angry that he made a careless mistake
They trust and support each other on the road
They plan to leave him behind in the desert
They do not have enough water to spare him
questions.why: The traders immediately share their water, showing the trust and support that holds the caravan together.

wrong.A: No anger is shown toward the man.
wrong.C: They help him rather than leaving him behind.
wrong.D: They do have enough water to share.

questions.stem: In the story, an oasis is most likely —
options: a kind of camel that needs no water
a strong wind that blows across sand
a place in the desert with water
a rock shaped like a camel's head
questions.why: The story mentions reaching a well or oasis, meaning a place where water can be found in the desert.

wrong.A: An oasis is not a kind of camel.
wrong.B: An oasis is not a type of wind.
wrong.D: The rock is a separate landmark, not an oasis.

questions.stem: Why does Faisal's father say trust between merchants keeps a caravan alive?
options: Because each merchant carries his own separate map
Because every merchant owns the exact same goods
Because the king demands that merchants trust each other
Because merchants must help each other to survive hardship
questions.why: The shared water after the leak shows that merchants depend on helping each other to get through hardship safely.

wrong.B: Merchants carry different goods, not identical ones.
wrong.C: No king is mentioned giving such an order.

keyWords.definition: to find and follow a safe way from one place to another
keyWords.example: Sailors once used the stars to navigate across the open ocean.

keyWords.definition: a sweet-smelling resin from certain trees, long valued and traded across Arabia
keyWords.example: Merchants carried frankincense along ancient desert routes to sell in distant markets.

keyWords.definition: absolutely necessary; something you cannot do without
keyWords.example: Clean water is essential for everyone's health.

keyWords.definition: to work together with others toward a shared goal
keyWords.example: The team had to cooperate closely to finish the project on time.

keyWords.definition: hard to find because there is very little of it
keyWords.example: Fresh vegetables were scarce in the village during the long winter.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says trusting other people matters more than being strong or clever on a hard journey. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about navigation, water, and cooperation.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that trust matters more than strength or cleverness on a hard journey like this one. Faisal's father was certainly skilled at navigating by the stars and landmarks, but that skill alone could not have saved the merchant whose water bag tore open; only the other traders' willingness to cooperate and share their scarce water kept him safe. Someone might argue that navigation skill was just as essential, since a lost caravan could never reach water at all, but even the best navigator depends on companions who will share resources and help each other through unexpected trouble.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the story?
options: Frankincense is more valuable than water in the desert, so the merchants spend most of their water on it, and the young man learns to buy it
A young merchant's first journey reveals how navigation, careful water use, and cooperation keep a caravan alive
Ancient incense routes were used by only one caravan, which crossed the desert once and never came back to the town again
Camels require no water when crossing the desert, so a caravan can travel for months without any supplies from the wells
questions.why: Faisal's reflection at the end ties together navigation, water management, and cooperation as the keys to surviving the journey.

wrong.A: Water proves essential, and its scarcity matters as much as the frankincense.
wrong.C: The route had been used by traders for centuries.
wrong.D: Camels still require carefully managed water in the story.

questions.stem: What valuable good does the caravan carry along the incense route?
options: Frankincense and cloth
Gold coins minted by a distant king
Fresh fruit grown near the coast
Tools used for building new wells
questions.why: The story states that the caravan carries bundles of frankincense and cloth between towns.

wrong.B: No gold coins are mentioned in the story.
wrong.C: Fresh fruit is not part of the caravan's cargo.

questions.stem: What does Faisal's father use, besides the stars, to navigate?
options: A compass brought from a distant kingdom by a trader
Letters left behind by earlier travelers in the sand
Landmarks, such as a distinctive rock formation
A map drawn by a royal geographer long ago
questions.why: The father explains that landmarks, like a rock shaped like a camel's head, help show the way along with the stars.

wrong.A: No compass is mentioned in the story.
wrong.B: No letters from earlier travelers appear.
wrong.D: No map or geographer is described.

questions.stem: In the story, essential most likely means —
options: completely unnecessary and easy to replace at any time
absolutely necessary and impossible to do without
extremely rare and valuable to merchants in the city
difficult to carry across long distances on camels
questions.why: The story explains that water is essential because the desert journey cannot be survived without it.

wrong.A: Essential is the opposite of unnecessary.
wrong.C: Rarity is not what the word essential describes here.
wrong.D: Difficulty of carrying is not the meaning emphasized.

questions.stem: Why does the sudden wind pose such a serious problem for the caravan?
options: It damages the frankincense the caravan is carrying
It frightens the camels into running away from the men
It uses up the limited water supply the caravan has
It hides the landmarks the men depend on to navigate
questions.why: The thick sand blocks the view of the landmarks the men rely on, forcing the caravan to stop until it clears.

wrong.A: Damage to the frankincense is not described.
wrong.B: The camels are not said to run away.
wrong.C: The wind itself does not use up water; the torn bag does.

questions.stem: Which of these events happened first?
options: Faisal's father taught him to navigate by the stars
The strong wind hid the horizon from view
The merchant's water bag was found to be torn
Faisal helped sell the frankincense at the market
questions.why: Faisal's father teaches him about the stars and landmarks before the wind, the torn bag, and the final sale occur.

wrong.B: The wind occurs after the father's lesson on navigation.
wrong.C: The torn bag is discovered only after the wind dies down.
wrong.D: Selling the frankincense happens at the very end of the journey.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about why the other traders shared water without being asked?
options: They had far more water than they truly needed for the trip
The man with the torn bag demanded their help right away
Cooperation and trust were expected among traveling merchants
Faisal's father ordered them to share their water
questions.why: The traders act immediately and without demand, reflecting a shared expectation of cooperation among merchants on the road.

wrong.A: Water is described as scarce, not plentiful.
wrong.B: No demand is made by the man with the torn bag.
wrong.D: Faisal's father explains the value of trust but does not give this specific order.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the story with Faisal's reflection beside the fire?
options: To show that Faisal regretted joining the caravan in the first place
To explain exactly how frankincense is harvested from the trees
To describe the market town in further detail for the readers
To emphasize the real lessons Faisal learned about trust and survival
questions.why: Faisal's closing thoughts tie together the navigation, water, and trust lessons that defined his first journey.

wrong.A: Faisal feels proud, not regretful, about the journey.
wrong.B: The harvesting of frankincense is not explained.
wrong.C: The market town itself is not described in further detail here.
